The Variational Method

What you need to know

  • The Schrödinger equation is solved exactly for the box, the spring, the rotor and the hydrogen atom, and for almost nothing else. Helium already has a term, the repulsion e2/4πε0r12e^2/4\pi\varepsilon_0 r_{12}e2/4πε0​r12​ between its two electrons, that no formula handles. Chemistry runs on two approximation methods: the variational method of this lecture and perturbation theory of the next two.

  • The variational theorem. Take any function ϕ\phiϕ that obeys the boundary conditions and compute its average energy. The result can never lie below the true ground-state energy: ⟨ϕ∣H^∣ϕ⟩/⟨ϕ∣ϕ⟩≥E0\langle\phi|\hat{H}|\phi\rangle/\langle\phi|\phi\rangle \geq E_0⟨ϕ∣H^∣ϕ⟩/⟨ϕ∣ϕ⟩≥E0​. Every guess gives an upper bound, so of two guesses the one with the lower energy is the better one.

  • The recipe. Put adjustable parameters in the guess, compute the energy as a function of them, and minimize. A Gaussian for hydrogen gives −0.424 Eh-0.424\,E_h−0.424Eh​ against the exact -0.5; a screened nuclear charge for helium gives ζ=27/16\zeta = 27/16ζ=27/16 and -77.5 eV against -79.0 eV.

  • The linear variational method. Write the guess as a sum of fixed basis functions, ϕ=∑ncnfn\phi = \sum_n c_nf_nϕ=∑n​cn​fn​, and vary only the coefficients. Minimizing turns the Schrödinger equation into the matrix problem Hc=E Sc\mathbf{H}\mathbf{c} = E\,\mathbf{S}\mathbf{c}Hc=ESc, solved by the secular determinant det⁡(H−E S)=0\det(\mathbf{H} - E\,\mathbf{S}) = 0det(H−ES)=0 or by one line of numpy. Adding basis functions can only lower the energy.

  • Two functions that mix give two levels pushed apart, E±E_\pmE±​: one below both starting energies and one above. This two-level problem returns as perturbation theory in Lecture 6.2, as absorption of light in Lecture 6.3 and as the chemical bond in Chapter 8. Every electronic-structure program solves the same equation with thousands of basis functions.

Where exact solutions stop¶

Four model systems have carried the course so far, and each was solved exactly:

systempotentialsolved in
particle in a boxwallsLecture 3.2
harmonic oscillator12kx2\frac{1}{2}kx^221​kx2Lecture 4.2
rigid rotornone, fixed distanceLecture 4.5
hydrogenlike atom−Ze2/4πε0r-Ze^2/4\pi\varepsilon_0 r−Ze2/4πε0​rLecture 5.1

The list ends there. Add one electron to hydrogen and the Hamiltonian of helium, written in the atomic units of Lecture 5.1 (ℏ=me=e=4πε0=1\hbar = m_e = e = 4\pi\varepsilon_0 = 1ℏ=me​=e=4πε0​=1), is

H^=−12∇12−2r1⏟electron 1    − 12∇22−2r2⏟electron 2  +  1r12⏟repulsion\hat{H} = \underbrace{-\tfrac{1}{2}\nabla_1^2 - \frac{2}{r_1}}_{\text{electron 1}}\;\;\underbrace{-\,\tfrac{1}{2}\nabla_2^2 - \frac{2}{r_2}}_{\text{electron 2}}\;+\;\underbrace{\frac{1}{r_{12}}}_{\text{repulsion}}H^=electron 1−21​∇12​−r1​2​​​electron 2−21​∇22​−r2​2​​​+repulsionr12​1​​​
(1)

The first two pieces are hydrogenlike atoms with Z=2Z = 2Z=2, which Lecture 5.1 solved. The last piece, the repulsion between the electrons a distance r12r_{12}r12​ apart, ties the coordinates of one electron to those of the other. The equation no longer separates, and no one has found a formula for its solutions. The same term appears between every pair of electrons in every atom and molecule.

Fig. The plan of the chapter. Beyond the exactly solved models there are two ways forward: guess the wavefunction and improve the guess (the variational method), or start from a solved problem and correct it step by step (perturbation theory). Both lead to the atoms and molecules of Chapters 7 and 8.

  • The variational method asks for a guess of the wavefunction. It returns an energy that is guaranteed to be too high, so guesses can be ranked and improved.

  • Perturbation theory asks for a solved problem close to the real one. It returns corrections to the energies and states, order by order (Lecture 6.2), and with a perturbation that changes in time it explains how light moves molecules between levels (Lecture 6.3).

An idea already used twice¶

Two earlier lectures found a ground-state energy by trying a family of states and keeping the one of lowest energy.

  • The spring (Lecture 4.2). Gaussians of every width σx\sigma_xσx​, centered in the well, have the average energy ℏ2/8μσx2+12kσx2\hbar^2/8\mu\sigma_x^2 + \frac{1}{2}k\sigma_x^2ℏ2/8μσx2​+21​kσx2​. The lowest value is 12ℏω\frac{1}{2}\hbar\omega21​ℏω, the zero-point energy.

  • The hydrogen atom (Lecture 5.1). Exponentials e−r/ae^{-r/a}e−r/a of every size aaa have the average energy ℏ2/2μa2−e2/4πε0a\hbar^2/2\mu a^2 - e^2/4\pi\varepsilon_0 aℏ2/2μa2−e2/4πε0​a. The lowest value is −12Eh=−13.6-\frac{1}{2}E_h = -13.6−21​Eh​=−13.6 eV, at a=a0a = a_0a=a0​.

Both answers were exact, because in each case the family happened to contain the true ground state. This lecture asks what the minimum means when it does not. The answer is the variational theorem: the minimum is then too high, and never too low.

The variational theorem¶

Any state is a mixture of the exact states¶

Let ϕ\phiϕ be any normalized function that obeys the boundary conditions of the problem: a guess, called a trial function. Its average energy is ⟨E⟩=⟨ϕ∣H^∣ϕ⟩\langle E\rangle = \langle\phi|\hat{H}|\phi\rangle⟨E⟩=⟨ϕ∣H^∣ϕ⟩. Three steps bound it from below.

  1. Expand the guess in the exact states. The eigenfunctions of H^\hat{H}H^ form a complete set (Lecture 3.6), whether or not anyone can write them down:

ϕ=∑ncn ψn,H^ψn=Enψn,E0≤E1≤E2≤…\phi = \sum_n c_n\,\psi_n, \qquad \hat{H}\psi_n = E_n\psi_n, \qquad E_0 \leq E_1 \leq E_2 \leq \dotsϕ=n∑​cn​ψn​,H^ψn​=En​ψn​,E0​≤E1​≤E2​≤…
(2)

Since ϕ\phiϕ is normalized, ∑n∣cn∣2=1\sum_n|c_n|^2 = 1∑n​∣cn​∣2=1.

  1. The average energy is a weighted average of the levels. A measurement of the energy returns EnE_nEn​ with probability ∣cn∣2|c_n|^2∣cn​∣2 (the Born rule of Lecture 3.6), so

⟨E⟩=⟨ϕ∣H^∣ϕ⟩=∑n∣cn∣2 En\langle E\rangle = \langle\phi|\hat{H}|\phi\rangle = \sum_n|c_n|^2\,E_n⟨E⟩=⟨ϕ∣H^∣ϕ⟩=n∑​∣cn​∣2En​
(3)

  1. An average cannot lie below its smallest entry. Every EnE_nEn​ is at least E0E_0E0​, so

⟨E⟩=∑n∣cn∣2 En  ≥  E0∑n∣cn∣2=E0\langle E\rangle = \sum_n|c_n|^2\,E_n \;\geq\; E_0\sum_n|c_n|^2 = E_0⟨E⟩=n∑​∣cn​∣2En​≥E0​n∑​∣cn​∣2=E0​
(4)

Here E0E_0E0​ stands for the lowest level, whatever its quantum number is called: n=1n = 1n=1 for the box and for hydrogen, v=0v = 0v=0 for the spring.

An energy measurement returns E1E_1E1​ in 68% of trials, E2E_2E2​ in 29%, higher levels in the rest. The average, 2.19 E12.19\,E_12.19E1​, lies above E1E_1E1​ because every single reading does.

The variational theorem
Eϕ=⟨ϕ∣H^∣ϕ⟩⟨ϕ∣ϕ⟩  ≥  E0E_\phi = \frac{\langle\phi|\hat{H}|\phi\rangle}{\langle\phi|\phi\rangle} \;\geq\; E_0Eϕ​=⟨ϕ∣ϕ⟩⟨ϕ∣H^∣ϕ⟩​≥E0​
(5)

  • ϕ\phiϕ is any trial function that obeys the boundary conditions, and E0E_0E0​ is the true ground-state energy

  • The denominator normalizes the guess; it is 1 if ϕ\phiϕ is already normalized

  • Equality holds only when ϕ\phiϕ is the true ground state ψ0\psi_0ψ0​

  • Every guess gives an upper bound. The true energy is never above the computed one. No knowledge of the exact solution is needed to say so.

  • Lower is better. Of two trial functions, the one with the lower EϕE_\phiEϕ​ is closer to the truth in energy. That turns guessing into a method: change the guess, keep the change if the energy drops.

  • The energy forgives a poor guess. Let the guess be the true ground state plus a small error, ϕ=ψ0+ϵ χ\phi = \psi_0 + \epsilon\,\chiϕ=ψ0​+ϵχ, with χ\chiχ normalized and orthogonal to ψ0\psi_0ψ0​. Then

Eϕ=E0+ϵ2 ⟨χ∣H^∣χ⟩1+ϵ2≈E0+ϵ2(⟨χ∣H^∣χ⟩−E0)E_\phi = \frac{E_0 + \epsilon^2\,\langle\chi|\hat{H}|\chi\rangle}{1 + \epsilon^2} \approx E_0 + \epsilon^2\left(\langle\chi|\hat{H}|\chi\rangle - E_0\right)Eϕ​=1+ϵ2E0​+ϵ2⟨χ∣H^∣χ⟩​≈E0​+ϵ2(⟨χ∣H^∣χ⟩−E0​)
(6)

An error of size ϵ\epsilonϵ in the function costs only ϵ2\epsilon^2ϵ2 in the energy. A guess that is 10% wrong can give an energy good to about 1%. The reverse also holds: a good energy does not certify the wavefunction, and other properties computed from it are less accurate.

  • The theorem is about the ground state. For an excited state the same argument works only if the trial function is orthogonal to every state below it. Symmetry can arrange that: an odd trial function in a symmetric well bounds the lowest odd state (Problem 7).

The recipe: guess, compute, minimize¶

  1. Guess. Choose a trial function ϕ\phiϕ with the right boundary conditions and a sensible shape: no more nodes than a ground state should have, large where the potential is low. Put adjustable parameters in it.

  2. Compute. Evaluate Eϕ=⟨ϕ∣H^∣ϕ⟩/⟨ϕ∣ϕ⟩E_\phi = \langle\phi|\hat{H}|\phi\rangle/\langle\phi|\phi\rangleEϕ​=⟨ϕ∣H^∣ϕ⟩/⟨ϕ∣ϕ⟩ as a function of the parameters.

  3. Minimize. Set the derivative with respect to each parameter to zero. The minimum is the best energy that family of functions can give, and it is still an upper bound.

One formula saves work in step 2. Integrating by parts, with ϕ\phiϕ vanishing at the ends of the range,

⟨ϕ∣T^∣ϕ⟩=−ℏ22m∫ϕ ϕ′′ dx=ℏ22m∫(ϕ′)2dx\langle\phi|\hat{T}|\phi\rangle = -\frac{\hbar^2}{2m}\int\phi\,\phi''\,dx = \frac{\hbar^2}{2m}\int\left(\phi'\right)^2dx⟨ϕ∣T^∣ϕ⟩=−2mℏ2​∫ϕϕ′′dx=2mℏ2​∫(ϕ′)2dx
(7)

so the kinetic energy needs only the first derivative: it is large wherever the function is steep.

No parameter: a parabola in a box¶

Example: guess the ground state of a box

A particle in a box of length LLL has the ground state 2/L sin⁡(πx/L)\sqrt{2/L}\,\sin(\pi x/L)2/L​sin(πx/L) with E1=π2ℏ2/2mL2E_1 = \pi^2\hbar^2/2mL^2E1​=π2ℏ2/2mL2. Pretend not to know it, and guess the simplest function that vanishes at both walls, ϕ=x(L−x)\phi = x(L - x)ϕ=x(L−x). What energy does the guess give?

Inside the box H^=−(ℏ2/2m) d2/dx2\hat{H} = -(\hbar^2/2m)\,d^2/dx^2H^=−(ℏ2/2m)d2/dx2, and ϕ′′=−2\phi'' = -2ϕ′′=−2, so H^ϕ=ℏ2/m\hat{H}\phi = \hbar^2/mH^ϕ=ℏ2/m, a constant. The two integrals are

⟨ϕ∣H^∣ϕ⟩=ℏ2m∫0Lx(L−x) dx=ℏ2L36m\langle\phi|\hat{H}|\phi\rangle = \frac{\hbar^2}{m}\int_0^L x(L - x)\,dx = \frac{\hbar^2L^3}{6m}⟨ϕ∣H^∣ϕ⟩=mℏ2​∫0L​x(L−x)dx=6mℏ2L3​
(8)
⟨ϕ∣ϕ⟩=∫0Lx2(L−x)2 dx=L530\langle\phi|\phi\rangle = \int_0^L x^2(L - x)^2\,dx = \frac{L^5}{30}⟨ϕ∣ϕ⟩=∫0L​x2(L−x)2dx=30L5​
(9)
Eϕ=ℏ2L3/6mL5/30=5ℏ2mL2=10π2 E1=1.013 E1E_\phi = \frac{\hbar^2L^3/6m}{L^5/30} = \frac{5\hbar^2}{mL^2} = \frac{10}{\pi^2}\,E_1 = 1.013\,E_1Eϕ​=L5/30ℏ2L3/6m​=mL25ℏ2​=π210​E1​=1.013E1​
(10)

The guess is 1.3% too high. It is above E1E_1E1​, as the theorem requires, and close to it because a parabola looks like half a sine wave.

            ha="center", fontsize=13)
    ax.text(0.5, 0.14, f"{err:.1f}% high" if err > 0.05 else f"{err:.4f}% high", ha="center", fontsize=12, color=CARDINAL)
    ax.set_xlim(-0.05, 1.05); ax.set_ylim(-0.04, 1.95)
    ax.set_xticks([0, 1]); ax.set_xticklabels(["0", "$L$"]); ax.set_yticks([])
    ax.spines["left"].set_visible(False); ax.spines["bottom"].set_visible(False); ax.tick_params(labelsize=12, length=0)

Fig. Three guesses (teal) for the ground state of a box, drawn over the exact one (gray), with the area between them in red. (a) A tent, with a kink in the middle. (b) The parabola of the example. (c) The parabola plus a second term, built below. Each energy lies above E1E_1E1​, and the closer the shape, the lower the energy.

  • The theorem ranks the guesses. The tent (Problem 1) is 21.6% high, the parabola 1.3%, the two-term function 0.0015%. No comparison with the exact answer was needed to put them in that order.

  • Shape decides. The tent overlaps the true state almost as well as the parabola does, but its kink is steep, and steepness is kinetic energy.

One parameter: hydrogen with a Gaussian¶

The ground state of hydrogen is e−r/a0e^{-r/a_0}e−r/a0​, with E1=−12EhE_1 = -\frac{1}{2}E_hE1​=−21​Eh​. Suppose the guess is a Gaussian instead, ϕ=e−αr2\phi = e^{-\alpha r^2}ϕ=e−αr2, with the exponent α\alphaα free. In atomic units H^=−12∇2−1/r\hat{H} = -\frac{1}{2}\nabla^2 - 1/rH^=−21​∇2−1/r, and the recipe runs as follows.

  1. Normalize. ⟨ϕ∣ϕ⟩=∫0∞e−2αr2 4πr2 dr=(π/2α)3/2\langle\phi|\phi\rangle = \int_0^\infty e^{-2\alpha r^2}\,4\pi r^2\,dr = (\pi/2\alpha)^{3/2}⟨ϕ∣ϕ⟩=∫0∞​e−2αr24πr2dr=(π/2α)3/2.

  2. Compute the two parts of the energy. The integrals are in the dropdown below; divided by the normalization they give

  • 15% too high, and above the exact value for every α\alphaα. No Gaussian reaches −12Eh-\frac{1}{2}E_h−21​Eh​, because no Gaussian is the true state.

  • What the Gaussian gets wrong. The true function has a cusp at the nucleus and a long tail e−re^{-r}e−r. The Gaussian is flat at the nucleus and its tail e−αr2e^{-\alpha r^2}e−αr2 dies too fast.

  • Why chemists use Gaussians anyway. Integrals over products of Gaussians centered on different atoms have simple formulas, and exponentials do not. The cure for the poor shape is to add several Gaussians together, which is the linear method below.

Going further: the integrals behind E(α)E(\alpha)E(α)

Three standard integrals do all the work, with b=2αb = 2\alphab=2α:

∫0∞r e−br2dr=12b,∫0∞r2e−br2dr=π4b3/2\int_0^\infty r\,e^{-br^2}dr = \frac{1}{2b}, \qquad \int_0^\infty r^2e^{-br^2}dr = \frac{\sqrt{\pi}}{4b^{3/2}}∫0∞​re−br2dr=2b1​,∫0∞​r2e−br2dr=4b3/2π​​
(14)
∫0∞r4e−br2dr=3π8b5/2\int_0^\infty r^4e^{-br^2}dr = \frac{3\sqrt{\pi}}{8b^{5/2}}∫0∞​r4e−br2dr=8b5/23π​​
(15)

For a function of rrr alone, ∇2ϕ=ϕ′′+2ϕ′/r\nabla^2\phi = \phi'' + 2\phi'/r∇2ϕ=ϕ′′+2ϕ′/r, which for the Gaussian is (4α2r2−6α) e−αr2(4\alpha^2r^2 - 6\alpha)\,e^{-\alpha r^2}(4α2r2−6α)e−αr2. Then

⟨ϕ∣T^∣ϕ⟩=−12∫0∞(4α2r2−6α)e−2αr2 4πr2 dr=3α2(π2α)3/2\langle\phi|\hat{T}|\phi\rangle = -\frac{1}{2}\int_0^\infty\left(4\alpha^2r^2 - 6\alpha\right)e^{-2\alpha r^2}\,4\pi r^2\,dr = \frac{3\alpha}{2}\left(\frac{\pi}{2\alpha}\right)^{3/2}⟨ϕ∣T^∣ϕ⟩=−21​∫0∞​(4α2r2−6α)e−2αr24πr2dr=23α​(2απ​)3/2
(16)
⟨ϕ∣V^∣ϕ⟩=−∫0∞1r e−2αr2 4πr2 dr=−πα\langle\phi|\hat{V}|\phi\rangle = -\int_0^\infty\frac{1}{r}\,e^{-2\alpha r^2}\,4\pi r^2\,dr = -\frac{\pi}{\alpha}⟨ϕ∣V^∣ϕ⟩=−∫0∞​r1​e−2αr24πr2dr=−απ​
(17)

Dividing each by ⟨ϕ∣ϕ⟩=(π/2α)3/2\langle\phi|\phi\rangle = (\pi/2\alpha)^{3/2}⟨ϕ∣ϕ⟩=(π/2α)3/2 gives ⟨T⟩=3α/2\langle T\rangle = 3\alpha/2⟨T⟩=3α/2 and ⟨V⟩=−22α/π\langle V\rangle = -2\sqrt{2\alpha/\pi}⟨V⟩=−22α/π​.

The recipe does not need a formula for the exact answer. Pick a well and tune the width of a Gaussian trial function; the dashed level is the exact ground state, solved numerically for comparison.

  • In the spring the family contains the exact state, and the teal level touches the dashed one at one width: the bound becomes an equality.

  • In the V-shaped well no Gaussian is exact. The best one stops 0.5% above the dashed level.

  • The Morse well is lopsided, and a Gaussian centered at the minimum cannot follow it. Move the center as well: a second parameter lowers the bound further.

Helium: a charge that is not 2¶

Helium is where the exact solutions stopped. Drop the repulsion 1/r121/r_{12}1/r12​ from its Hamiltonian, and what is left is a sum of two He+^++ Hamiltonians, one for each electron. A Hamiltonian that is a sum separates: the energies add and the wavefunctions multiply. Both electrons then sit in the 1s orbital of He+^++, e−2re^{-2r}e−2r in atomic units, and the state of the atom is the product

ϕ(r1,r2)=ψ1s(r1) ψ1s(r2)∝e−2r1 e−2r2\phi(r_1, r_2) = \psi_{1s}(r_1)\,\psi_{1s}(r_2) \propto e^{-2r_1}\,e^{-2r_2}ϕ(r1​,r2​)=ψ1s​(r1​)ψ1s​(r2​)∝e−2r1​e−2r2​
(18)

This independent-electron product is not an eigenfunction of the true Hamiltonian, which still contains the repulsion. It is a guess, and the variational method can improve it.

Example: the effective nuclear charge of helium

Keep the product of two 1s orbitals, but let the charge in the exponent be a parameter ζ\zetaζ in place of 2:

ϕ(r1,r2)=ζ3π e−ζr1 e−ζr2(atomic units)\phi(r_1, r_2) = \frac{\zeta^3}{\pi}\,e^{-\zeta r_1}\,e^{-\zeta r_2} \qquad\text{(atomic units)}ϕ(r1​,r2​)=πζ3​e−ζr1​e−ζr2​(atomic units)
(19)

The Hamiltonian keeps the true nuclear charge Z=2Z = 2Z=2. The average energy has three parts:

  • kinetic energy, ζ2/2\zeta^2/2ζ2/2 for each electron: ζ2\zeta^2ζ2 in all

  • attraction to the nucleus, −Zζ-Z\zeta−Zζ for each electron, since ⟨1/r⟩=ζ\langle 1/r\rangle = \zeta⟨1/r⟩=ζ in this orbital: −2Zζ-2Z\zeta−2Zζ in all

  • repulsion between the two clouds, ⟨1/r12⟩=58ζ\langle 1/r_{12}\rangle = \frac{5}{8}\zeta⟨1/r12​⟩=85​ζ (a standard integral; the dropdown below shows where it comes from)

E(ζ)=ζ2−2Zζ+58ζ=ζ2−278ζ(Z=2)E(\zeta) = \zeta^2 - 2Z\zeta + \tfrac{5}{8}\zeta = \zeta^2 - \tfrac{27}{8}\zeta \quad (Z = 2)E(ζ)=ζ2−2Zζ+85​ζ=ζ2−827​ζ(Z=2)
(20)
dEdζ=2ζ−278=0⟹ζ=2716=1.69\frac{dE}{d\zeta} = 2\zeta - \tfrac{27}{8} = 0 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \zeta = \frac{27}{16} = 1.69dζdE​=2ζ−827​=0⟹ζ=1627​=1.69
(21)
E=−(2716)2Eh=−2.848 Eh=−77.5 eVE = -\left(\frac{27}{16}\right)^2E_h = -2.848\,E_h = -77.5\ \text{eV}E=−(1627​)2Eh​=−2.848Eh​=−77.5 eV
(22)

  • Screening. The best charge is less than 2. Each electron spends part of its time between the other electron and the nucleus, so each sees a nucleus of charge about 1.69. The effective nuclear charge of general chemistry is a variational parameter.

Going further: where 58ζ\frac{5}{8}\zeta85​ζ comes from

Each electron in the orbital e−ζre^{-\zeta r}e−ζr is a round cloud of charge with the density ρ(r)=(ζ3/π) e−2ζr\rho(r) = (\zeta^3/\pi)\,e^{-2\zeta r}ρ(r)=(ζ3/π)e−2ζr. Electrostatics gives the potential that such a cloud creates at a distance rrr from its center:

φ(r)=1r−(ζ+1r)e−2ζr\varphi(r) = \frac{1}{r} - \left(\zeta + \frac{1}{r}\right)e^{-2\zeta r}φ(r)=r1​−(ζ+r1​)e−2ζr

Far away it is 1/r1/r1/r, the potential of a point charge; inside the cloud it is weaker, and at the center it levels off at ζ\zetaζ. The repulsion energy is the potential of one cloud averaged over the density of the other:

⟨1r12⟩=∫0∞φ(r) ρ(r) 4πr2 dr\left\langle\frac{1}{r_{12}}\right\rangle = \int_0^\infty\varphi(r)\,\rho(r)\,4\pi r^2\,dr⟨r12​1​⟩=∫0∞​φ(r)ρ(r)4πr2dr
(24)
=4ζ3∫0∞[r e−2ζr−(ζr2+r)e−4ζr]dr= 4\zeta^3\int_0^\infty\left[r\,e^{-2\zeta r} - \left(\zeta r^2 + r\right)e^{-4\zeta r}\right]dr=4ζ3∫0∞​[re−2ζr−(ζr2+r)e−4ζr]dr
(25)
=4ζ3[14ζ2−132ζ2−116ζ2]=58 ζ= 4\zeta^3\left[\frac{1}{4\zeta^2} - \frac{1}{32\zeta^2} - \frac{1}{16\zeta^2}\right] = \frac{5}{8}\,\zeta=4ζ3[4ζ21​−32ζ21​−16ζ21​]=85​ζ
(26)

Linear combinations: the method chemists use¶

Mix fixed functions¶

Nonlinear parameters such as α\alphaα and ζ\zetaζ sit inside exponentials, and each new one makes the minimization harder. A second kind of trial function avoids that. Choose a set of fixed functions f1,f2,…,fNf_1, f_2, \dots, f_Nf1​,f2​,…,fN​, the basis functions, and let only the mixing coefficients vary:

ϕ=c1f1+c2f2+⋯+cNfN\phi = c_1f_1 + c_2f_2 + \dots + c_Nf_Nϕ=c1​f1​+c2​f2​+⋯+cN​fN​
(27)

Minimizing the energy with respect to the coefficients needs no searching. It leads to a matrix eigenvalue problem, the kind Lecture 3.5 solved with eigh.

Two functions, step by step¶

Take N=2N = 2N=2 and real functions and coefficients.

  1. Write the energy. Insert ϕ=c1f1+c2f2\phi = c_1f_1 + c_2f_2ϕ=c1​f1​+c2​f2​ into E=⟨ϕ∣H^∣ϕ⟩/⟨ϕ∣ϕ⟩E = \langle\phi|\hat{H}|\phi\rangle/\langle\phi|\phi\rangleE=⟨ϕ∣H^∣ϕ⟩/⟨ϕ∣ϕ⟩ and multiply out:

E=c12H11+2c1c2H12+c22H22c12S11+2c1c2S12+c22S22E = \frac{c_1^2H_{11} + 2c_1c_2H_{12} + c_2^2H_{22}}{c_1^2S_{11} + 2c_1c_2S_{12} + c_2^2S_{22}}E=c12​S11​+2c1​c2​S12​+c22​S22​c12​H11​+2c1​c2​H12​+c22​H22​​
(28)
Hij=⟨fi∣H^∣fj⟩,Sij=⟨fi∣fj⟩H_{ij} = \langle f_i|\hat{H}|f_j\rangle, \qquad S_{ij} = \langle f_i|f_j\rangleHij​=⟨fi​∣H^∣fj​⟩,Sij​=⟨fi​∣fj​⟩
(29)

The HijH_{ij}Hij​ are the matrix elements of the Hamiltonian, the sandwiches of Lecture 3.5. The SijS_{ij}Sij​ are overlaps: the basis functions need not be orthogonal or normalized. H^\hat{H}H^ is Hermitian, so H12=H21H_{12} = H_{21}H12​=H21​.

  1. Minimize. Clear the fraction, E×(denominator)=numeratorE\times(\text{denominator}) = \text{numerator}E×(denominator)=numerator, and differentiate both sides with respect to c1c_1c1​. At the minimum ∂E/∂c1=0\partial E/\partial c_1 = 0∂E/∂c1​=0, which leaves

E(2c1S11+2c2S12)=2c1H11+2c2H12E\left(2c_1S_{11} + 2c_2S_{12}\right) = 2c_1H_{11} + 2c_2H_{12}E(2c1​S11​+2c2​S12​)=2c1​H11​+2c2​H12​
(30)

Collect the terms, and do the same for c2c_2c2​:

c1(H11−ES11)+c2(H12−ES12)=0c1(H12−ES12)+c2(H22−ES22)=0\begin{aligned} c_1\left(H_{11} - ES_{11}\right) + c_2\left(H_{12} - ES_{12}\right) &= 0\\ c_1\left(H_{12} - ES_{12}\right) + c_2\left(H_{22} - ES_{22}\right) &= 0 \end{aligned}c1​(H11​−ES11​)+c2​(H12​−ES12​)c1​(H12​−ES12​)+c2​(H22​−ES22​)​=0=0​
(31)

  1. Solve. These are two linear equations for c1c_1c1​ and c2c_2c2​. They always have the useless solution c1=c2=0c_1 = c_2 = 0c1​=c2​=0. Another solution exists only if the determinant of the coefficients vanishes, and that condition fixes EEE.

The linear variational method
ϕ=∑n=1Ncnfn⟹H c=E S c,det⁡(H−E S)=0\phi = \sum_{n=1}^N c_n f_n \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad \mathbf{H}\,\mathbf{c} = E\,\mathbf{S}\,\mathbf{c}, \qquad \det\left(\mathbf{H} - E\,\mathbf{S}\right) = 0ϕ=n=1∑N​cn​fn​⟹Hc=ESc,det(H−ES)=0
(32)
Hij=⟨fi∣H^∣fj⟩,Sij=⟨fi∣fj⟩H_{ij} = \langle f_i|\hat{H}|f_j\rangle, \qquad S_{ij} = \langle f_i|f_j\rangleHij​=⟨fi​∣H^∣fj​⟩,Sij​=⟨fi​∣fj​⟩
(33)

  • NNN basis functions give N×NN\times NN×N matrices and NNN roots. The lowest root is the best energy this basis can give, an upper bound to E0E_0E0​, and its eigenvector c\mathbf{c}c holds the best coefficients

  • det⁡(H−E S)=0\det(\mathbf{H} - E\,\mathbf{S}) = 0det(H−ES)=0 is the secular determinant

  • For an orthonormal basis S\mathbf{S}S is the identity, and the problem is the ordinary eigenvalue problem Hc=Ec\mathbf{H}\mathbf{c} = E\mathbf{c}Hc=Ec

  • numpy solves it in one line. eigh(H) handles an orthonormal basis, as in Lecture 3.5, and scipy.linalg.eigh(H, S) handles overlaps.

  • Adding a basis function never raises the lowest root. The old answer is still available, with the new coefficient set to zero, so the new minimum can only be equal or lower.

  • The higher roots are bounds too. Each is an upper bound to the corresponding excited level, the second root to the second level and so on.

The two-level problem¶

The smallest case, two orthonormal basis functions, is worth solving once and keeping: it returns in every remaining lecture of this chapter. Call the energies of the two functions E1=H11E_1 = H_{11}E1​=H11​ and E2=H22E_2 = H_{22}E2​=H22​, with E1≤E2E_1 \leq E_2E1​≤E2​, and the matrix element that connects them v=H12v = H_{12}v=H12​. The secular determinant is the quadratic equation (E1−E)(E2−E)−v2=0(E_1 - E)(E_2 - E) - v^2 = 0(E1​−E)(E2​−E)−v2=0.

The two-level problem
H=(E1vvE2),Δ=E2−E1\mathbf{H} = \begin{pmatrix} E_1 & v\\ v & E_2\end{pmatrix}, \qquad \Delta = E_2 - E_1H=(E1​v​vE2​​),Δ=E2​−E1​
(34)
E±=E1+E22±(Δ2)2+v2E_\pm = \frac{E_1 + E_2}{2} \pm \sqrt{\left(\frac{\Delta}{2}\right)^2 + v^2}E±​=2E1​+E2​​±(2Δ​)2+v2​
(35)

  • E1E_1E1​, E2E_2E2​: the energies of the two states before they mix. Δ\DeltaΔ: the gap between them. vvv: the coupling

  • Equal levels (Δ=0\Delta = 0Δ=0): E±=E1±∣v∣E_\pm = E_1 \pm |v|E±​=E1​±∣v∣, and the states mix half and half, (f1±f2)/2(f_1 \pm f_2)/\sqrt{2}(f1​±f2​)/2​

  • Distant levels (∣v∣≪Δ|v| \ll \Delta∣v∣≪Δ): E−≈E1−v2/ΔE_- \approx E_1 - v^2/\DeltaE−​≈E1​−v2/Δ and E+≈E2+v2/ΔE_+ \approx E_2 + v^2/\DeltaE+​≈E2​+v2/Δ, and the states barely mix

# left: the two diagonal elements, and the two roots they turn into
for y, lab in ((H11, "$E_1$"), (H22, "$E_2$")):
    ax.hlines(y, 0.0, 0.9, color=GRAY, lw=3.2)
    ax.text(-0.08, y, lab, ha="right", va="center", fontsize=14, color=GRAY)
for y, lab, col in ((Em, "$E_-$", TEAL), (Ep, "$E_+$", ORANGE)):
    ax.hlines(y, 1.9, 2.8, color=col, lw=3.2)
    ax.text(2.88, y, lab, ha="left", va="center", fontsize=14, color=col)
for y0, y1 in ((H11, Em), (H22, Ep)):
    ax.plot([0.9, 1.9], [y0, y1], color=GRAY, lw=1, ls=":")
ax.set_xlim(-0.75, 3.5); ax.set_ylim(-0.55, 1.55); ax.axis("off")
# right: the energy of cos(theta) f1 + sin(theta) f2
th = np.linspace(-90, 90, 721); t = np.radians(th)
E = H11 * np.cos(t) ** 2 + H22 * np.sin(t) ** 2 + H12 * np.sin(2 * t)
for y, col in ((H11, GRAY), (H22, GRAY), (Em, TEAL), (Ep, ORANGE)):

bx.plot(th, E, color="k", lw=2.8)
tp = np.degrees(0.5 * np.arctan2(2 * H12, H11 - H22))            # the angle of the highest mixture
tm = tp + 90 if tp < 0 else tp - 90                              # the lowest one is perpendicular to it
bx.plot([tm], [Em], "o", color=TEAL, ms=10, zorder=5); bx.plot([tp], [Ep], "o", color=ORANGE, ms=10, zorder=5)
bx.plot([0], [H11], "o", color=GRAY, ms=8, zorder=5); bx.plot([-90, 90], [H22, H22], "o", color=GRAY, ms=8, zorder=5, clip_on=False)
bx.text(tm, Em - 0.09, r"lowest", color=TEAL, fontsize=13, ha="center", va="top")
bx.text(tp, Ep + 0.07, r"highest", color=ORANGE, fontsize=13, ha="center", va="bottom")

bx.text(86, H22 + 0.06, r"$f_2$ alone", color=GRAY, fontsize=12.5, ha="right", va="bottom")

bx.set_xticks([-90, -45, 0, 45, 90]); bx.set_xticklabels(["-90°", "-45°", "0°", "45°", "90°"])
bx.set_yticks([]); bx.spines["left"].set_visible(False); bx.tick_params(labelsize=11.5)

Fig. The two-level problem. Left: the levels E1E_1E1​ and E2E_2E2​ before mixing, and the roots E−E_-E−​ and E+E_+E+​ after. Right: the energy of every normalized mixture cos⁡θ f1+sin⁡θ f2\cos\theta\,f_1 + \sin\theta\,f_2cosθf1​+sinθf2​. Its lowest and highest points are the two roots; f1f_1f1​ alone and f2f_2f2​ alone lie in between.

  • Mixing pushes the levels apart. E−E_-E−​ lies below both starting levels and E+E_+E+​ above both. The lower state gains exactly what the upper one loses.

  • The roots are the extremes of the energy. The curve on the right is the variational energy of every possible mixture. Finding its minimum and solving the eigenvalue problem are the same task.

  • Equal levels make the chemical bond. Two identical atomic orbitals on neighboring atoms have Δ=0\Delta = 0Δ=0. Chemists write their energy α\alphaα and their coupling β\betaβ, so the two levels are α±β\alpha \pm \betaα±β, and the lower mixture is the bond (Chapter 8).

  • Distant levels give perturbation theory. The small push v2/Δv^2/\Deltav2/Δ, coupling squared over gap, is the second-order shift of Lecture 6.2. Lecture 6.3 then drives the same two levels with light.

The box again, with two polynomials¶

Example: improve the parabola

Add a second function to the parabola of the first example: f1=x(L−x)f_1 = x(L - x)f1​=x(L−x) and f2=x2(L−x)2f_2 = x^2(L - x)^2f2​=x2(L−x)2. Find the best energy of ϕ=c1f1+c2f2\phi = c_1f_1 + c_2f_2ϕ=c1​f1​+c2​f2​.

With L=1L = 1L=1 and energies in units of ℏ2/mL2\hbar^2/mL^2ℏ2/mL2, the matrix elements are integrals of polynomials. Using Hij=12∫fi′fj′ dxH_{ij} = \frac{1}{2}\int f_i'f_j'\,dxHij​=21​∫fi′​fj′​dx:

H=(161301301105),S=(130114011401630)\mathbf{H} = \begin{pmatrix} \frac{1}{6} & \frac{1}{30}\\[2pt] \frac{1}{30} & \frac{1}{105}\end{pmatrix}, \qquad \mathbf{S} = \begin{pmatrix} \frac{1}{30} & \frac{1}{140}\\[2pt] \frac{1}{140} & \frac{1}{630}\end{pmatrix}H=(61​301​​301​1051​​),S=(301​1401​​1401​6301​​)
(36)

The functions overlap (S12≠0S_{12} \neq 0S12​=0), so the problem is Hc=E Sc\mathbf{H}\mathbf{c} = E\,\mathbf{S}\mathbf{c}Hc=ESc:

import numpy as np
from scipy.linalg import eigh

# f1 = x(1 - x) and f2 = x^2 (1 - x)^2, energies in units of hbar^2 / m L^2
H = np.array([[1/6, 1/30], [1/30, 1/105]])        # <f_i|H|f_j>
S = np.array([[1/30, 1/140], [1/140, 1/630]])     # overlaps <f_i|f_j>
E, C = eigh(H, S)                                 # solves H c = E S c
print("roots        :", np.round(E, 5))
print("exact E1, E3 :", np.round([np.pi**2 / 2, 9 * np.pi**2 / 2], 5))
print("c2 / c1      :", round(C[1, 0] / C[0, 0], 4))
roots        : [ 4.93487 51.06513]
exact E1, E3 : [ 4.9348  44.41322]
c2 / c1      : 1.1331

  • The lowest root is 4.93487, against the exact π2/2=4.93480\pi^2/2 = 4.93480π2/2=4.93480: 0.0015% too high. One extra function cut the error of the parabola by a factor of about 900. This is panel (c) of the figure above.

  • The second root, 51.07, is an upper bound to E3=44.41E_3 = 44.41E3​=44.41, not to E2E_2E2​. Both basis functions are symmetric about the middle of the box, so they can build only symmetric states, and the next symmetric state after ψ1\psi_1ψ1​ is ψ3\psi_3ψ3​.

Hydrogen from several Gaussians¶

One Gaussian gave hydrogen 85% of its binding energy. A sum of Gaussians with different exponents does better, and the coefficients come from the same matrix equation. For s-type Gaussians e−ar2e^{-ar^2}e−ar2 and e−br2e^{-br^2}e−br2 the matrix elements are known formulas (atomic units):

Sab=(πa+b)3/2,Hab=3aba+b Sab−2πa+bS_{ab} = \left(\frac{\pi}{a + b}\right)^{3/2}, \qquad H_{ab} = \frac{3ab}{a + b}\,S_{ab} - \frac{2\pi}{a + b}Sab​=(a+bπ​)3/2,Hab​=a+b3ab​Sab​−a+b2π​
(37)
alpha = np.array([0.15137, 0.68128, 4.5004])      # three exponents, in 1/a0^2
a, b = np.meshgrid(alpha, alpha)
S = (np.pi / (a + b))**1.5                        # overlaps
# kinetic energy plus Coulomb attraction, in hartree
H = 3 * a * b / (a + b) * S - 2 * np.pi / (a + b)
E, C = eigh(H, S)
print("lowest root:", round(E[0], 5), "hartree   (exact: -0.5)")
lowest root: -0.49698 hartree   (exact: -0.5)
Source
# synced: gaussian_basis
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from matplotlib.animation import FuncAnimation
from IPython.display import HTML

TEAL, CARDINAL, GRAY, PURPLE, ORANGE = "#107895", "#C8102E", "#6c757d", "#6a3d9a", "#e07b00"
from scipy.linalg import eigh
plt.rcParams.update({"axes.spines.top": False, "axes.spines.right": False})
sets = {1: [0.28294], 2: [0.20153, 1.3325], 3: [0.15137, 0.68128, 4.5004],     # best exponents for N Gaussians
        4: [0.12195, 0.44454, 1.9623, 13.011], 5: [0.10307, 0.32723, 1.1647, 5.1236, 34.061]}
r = np.linspace(0, 3.2, 600)
Es, curves = {}, {}
for N, al in sets.items():
    a, b = np.meshgrid(al, al)
    S = (np.pi / (a + b)) ** 1.5                                # overlap of exp(-a r^2) and exp(-b r^2)
    H = 3 * a * b / (a + b) * S - 2 * np.pi / (a + b)           # kinetic plus Coulomb, hartree
    E, C = eigh(H, S)
    Es[N] = E[0]
    curves[N] = abs(sum(c * np.exp(-e * r**2) for c, e in zip(C[:, 0], al)))
fig, (ax, bx) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(9.6, 4.2), gridspec_kw={"width_ratios": [1, 1.05], "wspace": 0.3})
ax.axhline(-0.5, color=GRAY, lw=1.6, ls=(0, (5, 3)))
ax.text(5.45, -0.5035, r"exact $-\frac{1}{2}$", color=GRAY, fontsize=13, ha="right", va="top")
for N, E in Es.items():
    ax.hlines(E, N - 0.32, N + 0.32, color=TEAL, lw=3.4)
    ax.text(N, E + 0.004, rf"${E:.4f}$", ha="center", va="bottom", fontsize=11.5, color=TEAL)
ax.set_xlim(0.45, 5.55); ax.set_ylim(-0.512, -0.41)
ax.set_xticks([1, 2, 3, 4, 5]); ax.set_yticks([-0.5, -0.48, -0.46, -0.44, -0.42]); ax.tick_params(labelsize=10.5)
ax.set_xlabel("number of Gaussians", fontsize=12.5); ax.set_ylabel(r"lowest root ($E_h$)", fontsize=12.5)
bx.plot(r, np.exp(-r) / np.sqrt(np.pi), color=GRAY, lw=4.5, alpha=0.55)
for N, ls in ((1, (0, (1, 1.5))), (2, (0, (4, 2))), (3, "-")):
    bx.plot(r, curves[N], color=TEAL, lw=2.2, ls=ls)
bx.text(0.2, 0.55, "exact", color=GRAY, fontsize=13, ha="left")
for N, (xx, yy) in ((1, (0.05, 0.245)), (2, (0.05, 0.385)), (3, (0.3, 0.475))):
    bx.text(xx, yy, f"{N}", color=TEAL, fontsize=13, ha="left", va="center")
bx.set_xlim(0, 3.2); bx.set_ylim(0, 0.6)
bx.set_xlabel(r"$r$ ($a_0$)", fontsize=12.5); bx.set_ylabel(r"$\psi(r)$", fontsize=12.5); bx.tick_params(labelsize=10.5)
fig.subplots_adjust(left=0.105, right=0.98, top=0.96, bottom=0.14)
plt.show()

Fig. Hydrogen from one to five Gaussians, each set with its best exponents. Left: the lowest root steps down toward the exact −12Eh-\frac{1}{2}E_h−21​Eh​ and never passes it. Right: the sums of one, two and three Gaussians against the exact e−r/a0e^{-r/a_0}e−r/a0​. Tight Gaussians build up the cusp at the nucleus.

  • Three Gaussians recover 99.4% of the energy, -0.4970 of -0.5 hartree, and five recover 99.96%.

  • This is a basis set. The name STO-3G on a quantum chemistry program’s menu means three Gaussians standing in for each exponential orbital, exactly as here.

  • Every electronic-structure program solves Hc=E Sc\mathbf{H}\mathbf{c} = E\,\mathbf{S}\mathbf{c}Hc=ESc. The basis functions are Gaussians on each atom, the matrices have thousands of rows, and the eigenvectors are the molecular orbitals (Hartree-Fock, Chapter 8).

The variational method needs a guess and returns a bound, with no estimate of how far above the truth the bound lies. When the problem is a small change to one that is already solved, no guess is needed: perturbation theory corrects the known answer directly.

Computational lab

Linear variational method builds H\mathbf{H}H and S\mathbf{S}S numerically for any well and any basis, in a Colab notebook.

Problems¶

Problem 1: A tent in a box¶

Use the tent function, ϕ=x\phi = xϕ=x for 0≤x≤L/20 \leq x \leq L/20≤x≤L/2 and ϕ=L−x\phi = L - xϕ=L−x for L/2≤x≤LL/2 \leq x \leq LL/2≤x≤L, as a trial function for the ground state of a particle in a box. Find EϕE_\phiEϕ​ and compare it with E1E_1E1​ and with the parabola of the first example.

Solution

The tent has a kink, so ϕ′′\phi''ϕ′′ is zero everywhere except at one point. Use the first-derivative form of the kinetic energy, ⟨ϕ∣H^∣ϕ⟩=(ℏ2/2m)∫(ϕ′)2dx\langle\phi|\hat{H}|\phi\rangle = (\hbar^2/2m)\int(\phi')^2dx⟨ϕ∣H^∣ϕ⟩=(ℏ2/2m)∫(ϕ′)2dx. The slope is +1 on the left half and -1 on the right, so (ϕ′)2=1(\phi')^2 = 1(ϕ′)2=1 throughout:

⟨ϕ∣H^∣ϕ⟩=ℏ22m L,⟨ϕ∣ϕ⟩=2∫0L/2x2 dx=L312\langle\phi|\hat{H}|\phi\rangle = \frac{\hbar^2}{2m}\,L, \qquad \langle\phi|\phi\rangle = 2\int_0^{L/2}x^2\,dx = \frac{L^3}{12}⟨ϕ∣H^∣ϕ⟩=2mℏ2​L,⟨ϕ∣ϕ⟩=2∫0L/2​x2dx=12L3​
(38)
Eϕ=ℏ2L/2mL3/12=6ℏ2mL2=12π2 E1=1.216 E1E_\phi = \frac{\hbar^2L/2m}{L^3/12} = \frac{6\hbar^2}{mL^2} = \frac{12}{\pi^2}\,E_1 = 1.216\,E_1Eϕ​=L3/12ℏ2L/2m​=mL26ℏ2​=π212​E1​=1.216E1​
(39)

The tent is 21.6% too high, against 1.3% for the parabola. Both obey the boundary conditions and both have one maximum in the middle, but the tent stays steep all the way to its peak, and ∫(ϕ′)2dx\int(\phi')^2dx∫(ϕ′)2dx counts steepness. The theorem ranks the parabola as the better guess without any reference to the exact solution.

Problem 2: A Lorentzian in a spring¶

Use ϕ=1/(x2+b2)\phi = 1/(x^2 + b^2)ϕ=1/(x2+b2), with bbb as the parameter, as a trial function for the ground state of the harmonic oscillator, H^=−(ℏ2/2μ) d2/dx2+12kx2\hat{H} = -(\hbar^2/2\mu)\,d^2/dx^2 + \frac{1}{2}kx^2H^=−(ℏ2/2μ)d2/dx2+21​kx2. Show that E(b)=ℏ2/4μb2+12kb2E(b) = \hbar^2/4\mu b^2 + \frac{1}{2}kb^2E(b)=ℏ2/4μb2+21​kb2, minimize it, and compare the result with 12ℏω\frac{1}{2}\hbar\omega21​ℏω. Why does this trial function do so much worse than a Gaussian? Useful integrals over all xxx:

∫dx(x2+b2)2=π2b3,∫x2 dx(x2+b2)2=π2b\int\frac{dx}{(x^2 + b^2)^2} = \frac{\pi}{2b^3}, \qquad \int\frac{x^2\,dx}{(x^2 + b^2)^2} = \frac{\pi}{2b}∫(x2+b2)2dx​=2b3π​,∫(x2+b2)2x2dx​=2bπ​
(40)
∫x2 dx(x2+b2)4=π16b5\int\frac{x^2\,dx}{(x^2 + b^2)^4} = \frac{\pi}{16b^5}∫(x2+b2)4x2dx​=16b5π​
(41)

Problem 3: Where the 1.3% comes from¶

The normalized parabola ϕ=30/L5 x(L−x)\phi = \sqrt{30/L^5}\,x(L - x)ϕ=30/L5​x(L−x) has the expansion coefficients cn=⟨ψn∣ϕ⟩=815/n3π3c_n = \langle\psi_n|\phi\rangle = 8\sqrt{15}/n^3\pi^3cn​=⟨ψn​∣ϕ⟩=815​/n3π3 for odd nnn and zero for even nnn in the states of the box. (a) Find the probabilities of measuring E1E_1E1​, E3E_3E3​ and E5E_5E5​. (b) Compute the average energy from ∑n∣cn∣2En\sum_n|c_n|^2E_n∑n​∣cn​∣2En​ and check it against the example. (c) How large is the error in the wavefunction, and how large is the error in the energy?

Solution

(a) ∣cn∣2=960/n6π6|c_n|^2 = 960/n^6\pi^6∣cn​∣2=960/n6π6 for odd nnn:

∣c1∣2=960π6=0.99856,∣c3∣2=∣c1∣2729=0.00137|c_1|^2 = \frac{960}{\pi^6} = 0.99856, \qquad |c_3|^2 = \frac{|c_1|^2}{729} = 0.00137∣c1​∣2=π6960​=0.99856,∣c3​∣2=729∣c1​∣2​=0.00137
(42)
∣c5∣2=∣c1∣215625=0.00006|c_5|^2 = \frac{|c_1|^2}{15625} = 0.00006∣c5​∣2=15625∣c1​∣2​=0.00006
(43)

The even states are missing because the parabola is symmetric about the middle of the box and they are antisymmetric.

(b) With En=n2E1E_n = n^2E_1En​=n2E1​,

⟨E⟩=∑n odd960n6π6 n2E1=960π6 E1∑n odd1n4\langle E\rangle = \sum_{n\ \text{odd}}\frac{960}{n^6\pi^6}\,n^2E_1 = \frac{960}{\pi^6}\,E_1\sum_{n\ \text{odd}}\frac{1}{n^4}⟨E⟩=n odd∑​n6π6960​n2E1​=π6960​E1​n odd∑​n41​
(44)
=960π6⋅π496 E1=10π2 E1=1.013 E1= \frac{960}{\pi^6}\cdot\frac{\pi^4}{96}\,E_1 = \frac{10}{\pi^2}\,E_1 = 1.013\,E_1=π6960​⋅96π4​E1​=π210​E1​=1.013E1​
(45)

the value found directly in the example. The first two terms alone give 0.99856+9×0.00137=1.01090.99856 + 9\times0.00137 = 1.01090.99856+9×0.00137=1.0109.

(c) The guess is 99.86% ground state. The part that is wrong has weight ϵ2=0.0014\epsilon^2 = 0.0014ϵ2=0.0014, an amplitude ϵ=0.038\epsilon = 0.038ϵ=0.038: the wavefunction is off by about 4%. The energy is off by 1.3%, which is ϵ2\epsilon^2ϵ2 times the cost of the admixed states, mostly ψ3\psi_3ψ3​ at 8E18E_18E1​ above the ground state: 0.00137×8=0.0110.00137\times8 = 0.0110.00137×8=0.011. The error in the energy is second order in the error of the function.

Problem 4: A V-shaped well¶

A particle moves in the well V(x)=F∣x∣V(x) = F|x|V(x)=F∣x∣. Use the Gaussian ϕ=e−ax2\phi = e^{-ax^2}ϕ=e−ax2 as a trial function. With ⟨T⟩=ℏ2a/2m\langle T\rangle = \hbar^2a/2m⟨T⟩=ℏ2a/2m and ⟨∣x∣⟩=1/2πa\langle|x|\rangle = 1/\sqrt{2\pi a}⟨∣x∣⟩=1/2πa​ for this function, write E(a)E(a)E(a), minimize it, and show that the best energy is 32(ℏ2F2/2πm)1/3=0.813 (ℏ2F2/m)1/3\frac{3}{2}\left(\hbar^2F^2/2\pi m\right)^{1/3} = 0.813\,(\hbar^2F^2/m)^{1/3}23​(ℏ2F2/2πm)1/3=0.813(ℏ2F2/m)1/3. The exact ground-state energy is 0.809 (ℏ2F2/m)1/30.809\,(\hbar^2F^2/m)^{1/3}0.809(ℏ2F2/m)1/3. How close is the bound, and which way is it off? Check your value against the widget above, which uses ℏ=m=F=1\hbar = m = F = 1ℏ=m=F=1.

Problem 5: Two orbitals that overlap¶

Two identical basis functions on neighboring atoms have H11=H22=αH_{11} = H_{22} = \alphaH11​=H22​=α, H12=βH_{12} = \betaH12​=β and an overlap S12=SS_{12} = SS12​=S, with S11=S22=1S_{11} = S_{22} = 1S11​=S22​=1. Solve the secular determinant and find the two energies and their coefficients. Which level moves farther from α\alphaα?

Solution

The secular determinant is

∣α−Eβ−ESβ−ESα−E∣=(α−E)2−(β−ES)2=0\begin{vmatrix}\alpha - E & \beta - ES\\ \beta - ES & \alpha - E\end{vmatrix} = (\alpha - E)^2 - (\beta - ES)^2 = 0∣∣​α−Eβ−ES​β−ESα−E​∣∣​=(α−E)2−(β−ES)2=0
(46)
α−E=±(β−ES)\alpha - E = \pm(\beta - ES)α−E=±(β−ES)
(47)
E+=α+β1+S,E−=α−β1−SE_+ = \frac{\alpha + \beta}{1 + S}, \qquad E_- = \frac{\alpha - \beta}{1 - S}E+​=1+Sα+β​,E−​=1−Sα−β​
(48)

Insert each root into the first equation, c1(α−E)+c2(β−ES)=0c_1(\alpha - E) + c_2(\beta - ES) = 0c1​(α−E)+c2​(β−ES)=0. For E+E_+E+​, α−E=−(β−ES)\alpha - E = -(\beta - ES)α−E=−(β−ES) and so c1=c2c_1 = c_2c1​=c2​: the mixture f1+f2f_1 + f_2f1​+f2​. For E−E_-E−​, c1=−c2c_1 = -c_2c1​=−c2​: the mixture f1−f2f_1 - f_2f1​−f2​.

With S=0S = 0S=0 the levels are α±β\alpha \pm \betaα±β, split evenly. With an overlap, measure both from α\alphaα:

E+−α=β−αS1+S,E−−α=−β−αS1−SE_+ - \alpha = \frac{\beta - \alpha S}{1 + S}, \qquad E_- - \alpha = -\frac{\beta - \alpha S}{1 - S}E+​−α=1+Sβ−αS​,E−​−α=−1−Sβ−αS​
(49)

The two shifts have the same numerator and opposite signs, but the second is divided by the smaller number 1−S1 - S1−S. For a bond, β−αS\beta - \alpha Sβ−αS is negative: f1+f2f_1 + f_2f1​+f2​ is the bonding orbital, lowered by ∣β−αS∣/(1+S)|\beta - \alpha S|/(1 + S)∣β−αS∣/(1+S), and f1−f2f_1 - f_2f1​−f2​ is the antibonding orbital, raised by the larger amount ∣β−αS∣/(1−S)|\beta - \alpha S|/(1 - S)∣β−αS∣/(1−S). That asymmetry is why filling both orbitals, as in He2_22​, gives no bond (Chapter 8).

Problem 6: Two-electron ions¶

The helium example gives E(ζ)=ζ2−2Zζ+58ζE(\zeta) = \zeta^2 - 2Z\zeta + \frac{5}{8}\zetaE(ζ)=ζ2−2Zζ+85​ζ hartree for any nucleus of charge ZZZ with two electrons. (a) Show that the best exponent is ζ=Z−516\zeta = Z - \frac{5}{16}ζ=Z−165​ and the best energy −(Z−516)2-(Z - \frac{5}{16})^2−(Z−165​)2. (b) Evaluate it for H−^-− (Z=1Z = 1Z=1) and Li+^++ (Z=3Z = 3Z=3) and compare with the exact energies, -0.5278 and -7.2799 hartree. Problem 7: A bound for an excited state¶

The first excited state of the box, ψ2\psi_2ψ2​, is antisymmetric about the middle. Use the antisymmetric trial function ϕ=x(L−x)(L/2−x)\phi = x(L - x)(L/2 - x)ϕ=x(L−x)(L/2−x) to bound E2E_2E2​. Why is the result an upper bound to E2E_2E2​ and not merely to E1E_1E1​?

Solution

Set L=1L = 1L=1 and use units of ℏ2/mL2\hbar^2/mL^2ℏ2/mL2. Then ϕ∝x(1−x)(1−2x)=x−3x2+2x3\phi \propto x(1 - x)(1 - 2x) = x - 3x^2 + 2x^3ϕ∝x(1−x)(1−2x)=x−3x2+2x3 and ϕ′=1−6x+6x2\phi' = 1 - 6x + 6x^2ϕ′=1−6x+6x2:

∫01(ϕ′)2dx=1−6+16−18+365=15\int_0^1(\phi')^2dx = 1 - 6 + 16 - 18 + \frac{36}{5} = \frac{1}{5}∫01​(ϕ′)2dx=1−6+16−18+536​=51​
(50)
∫01ϕ2 dx=13−32+135−2+47=1210\int_0^1\phi^2\,dx = \frac{1}{3} - \frac{3}{2} + \frac{13}{5} - 2 + \frac{4}{7} = \frac{1}{210}∫01​ϕ2dx=31​−23​+513​−2+74​=2101​
(51)
Eϕ=12⋅151210=21 ℏ2mL2,E2=4π22 ℏ2mL2=19.74 ℏ2mL2E_\phi = \frac{\frac{1}{2}\cdot\frac{1}{5}}{\frac{1}{210}} = 21\,\frac{\hbar^2}{mL^2}, \qquad E_2 = \frac{4\pi^2}{2}\,\frac{\hbar^2}{mL^2} = 19.74\,\frac{\hbar^2}{mL^2}Eϕ​=2101​21​⋅51​​=21mL2ℏ2​,E2​=24π2​mL2ℏ2​=19.74mL2ℏ2​
(52)

The bound is 6.4% high. It bounds E2E_2E2​ because ϕ\phiϕ is antisymmetric about the middle of the box, and every symmetric state, ψ1\psi_1ψ1​ included, is orthogonal to it. In the expansion ϕ=∑cnψn\phi = \sum c_n\psi_nϕ=∑cn​ψn​ only the antisymmetric states n=2,4,6,…n = 2, 4, 6, \dotsn=2,4,6,… appear, and the lowest of them is ψ2\psi_2ψ2​. The proof of the theorem then runs as before, with E2E_2E2​ in the role of the lowest level.
